title: Meditation as practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth perfection: effort, tuned like a lute string, neither too tight nor too loose. Did you do one thing with glad effort? Day one thousand four hundred three.

A man has been starving himself in the forest for a long time. In the story, he eats so little that when he touches his belly he can feel his spine. He holds his breath until there is a roaring in his ears. Nothing he is looking for comes. And then, worn down to almost nothing, he remembers an afternoon from when he was a small boy. His father was at work in the fields. The boy was sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind went quiet and glad all by itself. The man is the future Buddha. The memory changes his whole path. Today, the fifth perfection: meditation.
screen: `STARVING HIMSELF IN THE FOREST.` → `A BOY UNDER A ROSE-APPLE TREE.` → `THE MEMORY THAT CHANGED THE PATH.`

segments.voice: In the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha tells this himself. Remembering the rose-apple tree, he asks: could that be the way to awakening? And he answers: that is the way. Then he asks why he should be afraid of a happiness that has nothing to do with sense pleasures and nothing to do with unwholesome things. He decides not to be afraid of it. He eats a little rice, gets his strength back, and sits. Notice what the story says about meditation. It does not start with force. It starts with a calm he already knew, and a willingness to trust it. The Pali word for those deep absorptions is jhana. In Sanskrit it is dhyana, and in the Mahayana list of perfections dhyana is the fifth: meditative steadiness, a mind that can stay. Tradition says the name of the Chan school in China, Zen in Japan, comes from this same word. Now the second side of it: steady, daily. At the close of one teaching in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha puts it plainly. Here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't be careless, or you'll regret it later. He points at an ordinary place and says, sit there. The perfection is not one great sitting. It is the habit of sitting, the way a path through a field is made by walking it every day. A long sitting now and then is good. A short one every day wears the path in.
screen: `THE MEMORY OF THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` · `NO NEED TO FEAR THAT CALM.` · `DHYANA, THE FIFTH PERFECTION.` · then, large: `THE ROOTS OF TREES: SIT THERE.`

segments.voice: For the next two minutes, if you'd like, find your own patch of shade. Sit with your back easy and upright, hands resting. Let the breath come and go without managing it. When the mind wanders, and it will, notice where it went and come back, the way the Buddha came back to a memory of a quiet afternoon. No need to force anything. Before you get up, pick one time later today or this week when you could sit for twenty minutes, and put it somewhere you'll see it. The bell holds the time.
Meditation as practice. Dhyana, the fifth perfection: a steady mind, built by sitting a little every day. Today's word.
Your line: the fifth perfection. Today, find one patch of shade, a bench, a parked car, a quiet stair, and sit there for a few breaths before you move on. Day one thousand four hundred three.

howItsDone: Buddhists in many schools keep a daily sitting practice at home or in a temple, often at the same time each day; in the Mahayana list of six perfections, meditation (dhyana) is the fifth.

fork.setup: you're the future Buddha, worn thin by fasting. you remember a quiet afternoon in the shade as a boy. what do you do?
options: trust that calm, eat a little and sit.
give up the search and go home.
fork.reveal: he says to himself, that is the way, decides not to fear that happiness, eats some rice and sits.

original.note: Sanskrit dhyana (Pali jhana): meditative absorption; the fifth of the six perfections in the Mahayana list.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means forcing your mind to go blank.
what it means: dhyana, a steady, settled mind, trusted rather than forced, and built by sitting daily.
what a scholar hears: the rose-apple memory in the Middle Length Discourses, and the line 'here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts' at the close of the Discourse on Two Kinds of Thought.

notes: MN 36 paraphrased: extreme fasting (feeling the spine through the belly), breathless meditation with roaring in the head, the rose-apple memory while his father (the Sakyan) was working, 'that is the path to awakening', not fearing pleasure apart from sensuality, taking solid food. Confirm the order and wording; 'years' of austerities is not stated in MN 36 itself and could be softened.
'The roots of trees, empty huts; meditate, do not be negligent, lest you regret it later' paraphrased from MN 19 and other closing passages; confirm citation.
Chan/Zen name derived from dhyana framed as 'tradition says'; it is standard but is an etymology claim. Confirm or cut.
Index practice is 'sit twenty minutes'; the app sit is two minutes, so the practice invites scheduling a twenty-minute sit later.
